title: Optimization for deep learning, from first principles
lede: A guided journey from "we want the loss to be small" to the questions the papers in this Atlas answer. Every stop starts with a problem, builds the math that solves it from scratch, and lets you play with it: every surface is a real function and every ball runs a real optimizer. Dotted words are terms; hover or tap them for a plain-words definition.

chapters.title: The goal: make the loss small
chapters.question: What does "training a model" actually mean, and why can't we just solve for the answer?

chapters.title: Which way is down?
chapters.question: Standing at one point of a landscape we cannot see, how do we know which direction lowers the loss?

chapters.title: How far to step
chapters.question: Too small a step wastes time, too large a step blows up. What decides the right size, and what can we guarantee?

chapters.title: Curvature: how the landscape bends
chapters.question: Why does gradient descent zig-zag in long valleys, and how do we describe bending in many dimensions?

chapters.title: A zoo of flat points
chapters.question: A zero gradient means "flat", not "done". Which flat points are traps, and how do papers tell them apart?

chapters.title: Escaping saddle points
chapters.question: Gradient descent can crawl past saddles for a very long time. Is it ever truly stuck, and how do we get out faster?

chapters.title: Giving the optimizer memory
chapters.question: Zig-zags cancel and slow directions build up speed if the optimizer remembers its past steps. How much does memory buy?

chapters.title: Noise: stochastic gradients
chapters.question: A full gradient over millions of examples is too expensive. What happens when we use a noisy estimate instead?

chapters.title: A step size for every direction
chapters.question: One learning rate cannot suit every direction. What if each parameter gets its own?

chapters.title: Sharp and flat minima
chapters.question: There are many minima. Which one does training find, and does it matter which?

chapters.title: Why big networks are easier to train
chapters.question: Neural-network losses are non-convex, yet training usually works. What is special about their landscapes?

chapters.title: How hard can it be?
chapters.question: What is the best any algorithm could possibly do, and how close do the methods in the Atlas come?
